findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage have no one-time-use tracking
findings.body: isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks whether the submitted code exists in the stored raw list (`generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(...)`) and never removes/marks the matching code as used, nor is there any subsequent call anywhere in the authentication flow (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.action) that writes back a 'used' state to the user-storage provider after a successful login. Since getCredentials()/isValid() always reconstruct the credential model from the same unchanged raw code list stored in credentialData, every recovery code remains valid forever for users whose recovery codes live in this storage provider, defeating the single-use guarantee that recovery codes are supposed to provide. This is a real security/data-integrity regression introduced together with the feature that lets recovery codes be created in user storage, and the reference provider shipped in this PR demonstrates the gap without addressing it.

findings.title: getCredentials() can NPE when user is not found in the backing map
findings.body: getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel) calls `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` and then immediately dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes` without a null check. Every other method in this class that uses getMyUser() (e.g. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, isConfiguredFor) explicitly guards against `myUser == null` before accessing its fields. If getMyUser returns null here (user removed concurrently, race, or lookup inconsistency), this will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty/partial credential stream.

findings.title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are forwarded to the user-storage provider
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential builds `UserCredentialModel recoveryCodesCredential` from `recoveryCodesJson`, which is the plain JSON serialization of the raw generated codes (`generatedCodes`), not the hashed representation used by `credentialModel` for local storage. This value is passed verbatim to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, which the companion test provider (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage) stores and compares as-is, i.e. in plaintext. Unlike the local-DB path where RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel stores hashed codes, any user-storage implementation that persists the UserCredentialModel's challenge response directly (as the shipped reference implementation does) will store one-time recovery codes unhashed at rest, weakening the security of the feature for federated users.

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById likely cannot remove a user-storage-backed recovery codes credential
findings.body: When all recovery codes have been used, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. For credentials that are now newly supported to live in user storage (per this PR), the id returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() comes from the federated provider (e.g. a synthetic id generated by the test storage provider), not from the local credential store. removeStoredCredentialById is historically scoped to credentials persisted in the local DB store; it is not guaranteed to propagate removal to an external UserStorageProvider. Consequently the exhausted recovery-codes credential may silently remain configured in the user-storage provider even though the authenticator believes it removed it, leaving a stale/exhausted credential rather than cleanly forcing re-setup.

findings.title: No test coverage for recovery-code exhaustion/removal or disabling when stored in user storage
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only exercises generating recovery codes and performing a single successful login with one code against the new user-storage-backed credential path. There is no test verifying that codes become single-use (cannot be reused), that the credential is properly removed/replaced once all codes are consumed, or that admin/account REST credential disable operations behave correctly for a recovery-codes credential stored in user storage (unlike the analogous OTP tests testDisableCredentialsInUserStorage / testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin). Given the new behavior this PR introduces, these scenarios should be covered to catch regressions like unlimited code reuse.
